story.name: トウキョウ ひとりぐらし
story.title: Number Forty-Two
story.line: ブーケが くやくしょで じゅうしょを とどけます
story.ja: 日本では引っ越したら2週間以内に区役所へ届けを出す。月曜の朝、ブーケはアリゲッティの傘をさして区役所へ。案内のモーリーに言われて番号札（42番）を取り、用紙に記入して待つ。住所の書き方が逆で、日本は大きい方から書くと教わって書きなおすと、在留カードの裏に新しい住所が印字される。次は国民健康保険の窓口でまた番号札。同僚のチッチからは「次は本と、おやつを持っていって」。お昼までかかったけれど、新しい保険証を手にして大満足。傘を忘れてモーリーが走って届けてくれる。帰って返しに行くと、アリゲッティは土曜まで留守。トマトの水やりをたのむ書き置きがあった。

segments.en: In Japan, when you move, you have to tell the ward office within two weeks. Rosie had a reminder on her phone, with three exclamation points.
So on Monday morning, she took a few hours off work and walked to the ward office by the station. It was raining again.
She took Gayle's umbrella. Of course she did. It was the only umbrella she had.
The ward office was a big, busy building, full of signs, counters, and people waiting quietly in rows of chairs.
Rosie stood in the middle of the lobby and turned around slowly, like someone looking for their car in a parking lot.
A man at the information desk waved her over. He had a neat tie, a big smile, and a name tag: Orville.
Good morning! Welcome! How can I help you? Please, don't be shy. I'm practicing my English. I love to practice.
Hi! I just moved here, and I think I need to register my address? I'm sorry, I don't really know how this works.
No problem at all. First, please take a number from the machine. Then fill out this form, and have a seat.
The machine gave her a little paper ticket. Number forty-two. The screen above the counters said number twenty-nine.
Okay. Thirteen people ahead of me. That's fine. I've got a pen. I've got a form. I can do this.
The form had a lot of boxes. Name. Date of birth. Old address. New address. She filled them all out carefully, in her neatest handwriting.
When number forty-two came up, Orville was at the counter, and he seemed very happy to see her again.
Ah, it's you! Let me see. Very good. Very good. Oh. Oh, I see. Your address is the other way around.
The other way around? What do you mean?
In America, you start small. Your apartment, your street, your city. In Japan, we start big. Tokyo first. Then the ward, the neighborhood, the block, then your building.
Oh, that's funny. It's like zooming in on a map instead of out. Okay, give me one second.
She wrote it all again, from big to small. Orville checked every line with his finger, nodding at each one.
Then he printed her new address on the back of her residence card and handed it to her with both hands.
Perfect. Now, one more thing. Health insurance. That's a different counter, over there on the right. Please take another number.
Another number? Okay. Sure. Why not.
The second number was fifty-eight. She sat down again. The lady next to her was knitting a tiny sweater. The man on her other side was asleep.
She texted Nana, her coworker at the design studio in Ebisu, who had lived in Tokyo for years. Nana sent a voice message back.
Oh, the ward office! I remember. Next time, bring a book. And snacks. Don't worry, it's always slow, but it always works out.
By the time she had her insurance card, it was almost one o'clock. It had taken all morning.
But walking outside with a brand new card in her bag, she felt like she had won a prize.
Excuse me! Rosie! Wait, please! Your umbrella! You forgot your umbrella!
Orville came running down the front steps, holding Gayle's big navy umbrella over his head like a flag.
Oh my gosh, thank you! It's not even mine. My neighbor would never forgive me. I owe you one, Orville.
You're welcome. And welcome to the neighborhood. Now it's official. You're on paper! Have a nice day!
For lunch, she found a tiny restaurant with plastic food in the window, and pointed at the grilled fish. It came with rice, soup, and pickles.
On the way home, the rain stopped. She went straight to Gayle's door to give back the umbrella. She knocked. Nobody answered.
There was only a little note on the door, in neat handwriting. Visiting my sister. Back on Saturday. Could you water my tomatoes? G.
So Rosie watered the tomatoes, and carried the umbrella back upstairs. And that night, she stuck ticket number forty-two on her fridge.

ph.trap: 数を取る ではなく、順番待ちの札を取る
アメリカ英語は fill out。fill in も通じる
席を持つ ではなく「座ってください」の丁寧な言い方
別の道をまわる ではなく、順番や向きが逆
もうひとつの物 ではなく、話を追加する合図
work out＝運動する の意味もあるが、ここは「うまくいく」

ph.ja: ひとつ借りができたね
ph.trap: お金の借り ではなく、気軽なお礼

predict.ask: どようび、ブーケは どこへ いく？
choices: To the shrine festival on her own street.
Back to the ward office, for a third number.
To the airport, to pick up her mom.
predict.ja: 自分の家の通りでひらかれる神社のお祭りへ。
